nodes.question: How does dynamic LCIA differ from traditional assessments?
nodes.answer: Dynamic LCIA investigates time-dependent environmental impacts, considering the timing of greenhouse emissions.
nodes.paragraph: (2022a, b) developed GWP100 ranges. Carcassi et al. (2022) based their work on a specific (bamboo) product and developed three end-of-life scenarios for a novel mycelium insulation. The uniqueness of the study was to implement a dynamic LCIA that accounts for the growth and cultivation of bamboo used for the insulation manufacturing. However, the focus of Cascione et al. (2022a, b) and Carcassi et al. (2022) is limited to greenhouse emissions. Other emissions as listed in EN (2012) were not explored. Current LCA standards, EN 15804(2012) + A2(2019), do not take into account the timing for when emissions occur. Therefore, the temporary sequestration of carbon in bio-based materials and the temporary reduction of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere are not considered. Similar to Hawkins et al. (2021), Carcassi et al. (2022) presented a dynamic LCIA that considers the timings of green-house emissions. Dynamic life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) is an approach that investigates time-dependent environmental impacts (Levasseur n.d.).

nodes.question: What method is suggested for assessing the environmental impacts associated with biogas production?
nodes.answer: Life cycle assessment (LCA) is suggested as a suitable method for assessing the environmental impacts.
nodes.paragraph: Due to the widespread use of cover crops, including legumes, in organic farming, an organic dairy farm was chosen for a case study in the present study. Aside from the clear benefits with increased biogas production, the use of energy crops in biogas production may also have adverse effects related to changes in land use and soil carbon storage, as well as increased energy inputs for harvesting, transport and processing (Hamelin et al. 2014). These effects vary depending on the feedstock and case-specific factors (Hamelin et al. 2014; Hijazi et al. 2016) and the overall environmental consequences of such com- bined effects are insufficiently understood in the case of cover crop harvesting and co-digestion. Therefore, it is essential to assess the total environmental impact of the system to ensure that the use of cover crop in anaerobic digestion leads to reduced environmental impacts, for which life cycle assessment (LCA) is a suitable method. The objective of this study was to provide a com- prehensive assessment of the environmental impacts of biogas production at organic dairy farms, focus- ing on the co-digestion of cattle manure with silage of cover crops and straw.

nodes.question: What do LCA studies often omit regarding system-level uncertainties?
nodes.answer: LCA studies often omit rigorous evaluation of system-level uncertainties.

Theoretically speaking, uncertainties in carbon footprint estimates can arise from either of the two compu- tational stages of LCA, namely, life cycle inventory analysis (LCI) and life cycle impact assessment (LCIA). Within the context of livestock production systems, however, the choice of LCIA methodology has been shown to impart negligible effects on global warming potential as long as the timescale of analysis (e.g. 20 years, 100 years, or 500 years) is clearly defined (Reckmann 2013). Uncertainties associated with LCI, on the other hand, have considerable impacts on envi- ronmental footprints arising from different farming systems (McAuliffe et al. 2017) and are also of relevance to a large population of practitioners around the world.
